extracted.intended_audience: landscape painters, art students, and art critics interested in truthful representation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for representing landscape (especially distance, foreground detail, and skies) truthfully and effectively in painting and drawing, with examples drawn from Turner, Claude, Poussin, Canaletto, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering of distant detail as unified mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: In distant views, countless separate lines and details should appear as an intelligible whole rather than as distinct elements: "Not one line out of the millions there is without meaning, yet there is not one which is not affected and disguised by the dazzle and indecision of distance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: From a distance Westminster Abbey looks like "a building enriched with multitudinous vertical lines" which one cannot distinguish individually; Turner renders this 'mystery of decided line'—distinct, sharp, visible, but unintelligible—whereas the old masters either reduced distant detail to mere shadows or caricatured it with distinct lines (both being false and offensive). Aim to convey multitudinous richness without attempting to delineate single distant lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid distinct, precise lines in distant architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not render distant architectural elements with precise, delicate linear definition; such distinctness destroys the sense of distance and scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: the old masters giving principal lines with delicate clearness—produces a drawing of a model, not a building. Instead, retain uncertainty and mystery in distant architectural detail to preserve space and size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imply near architectural ornament rather than delineate every line
rubrics_metrics.description: Even for near architectural decoration, many of the carved lines are not individually visible; the painter should suggest richness and variety without resolving single engraved lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Capitals in St. Mark's appear exquisitely rich yet you 'cannot' tell the direction of a single line. Canaletto reduces such detail to dots (insufficient); the architect's precise drawing is also wrong. Turner’s capital in the foreground of Daphne and Leucippus gives disorderly lines that make the viewer 'feel in an instant that all are there.' Aim to imply pattern and diversity without literal delineation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreground landscape: pursue fulness of detail, rightly arranged and massed
rubrics_metrics.description: In landscape, it is 'impossible to go too fine, or think too much about details,' provided they are rightly arranged and massed; nature's decoration is ceaseless and incomparable and demands careful attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finish and detail are more necessary in landscape than in historical subjects. The detail of a weedy bank surpasses carved work; every leaf and stalk has tracery. However, such detail should be attained through appropriate means (see swift execution) and must be organized into coherent masses so that fulness does not become confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space and size require obscurity/obscure fulness; avoid vacancy and over-distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression of space and size depends on obscurity united with fulness; both vacancy (no measure) and distinctness (false measures) destroy the perception of space and size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Poussin's vacant distances give no measure and therefore no vivid impression; Hobbima's middle distance contradicts perspective by too much distinctness. Preserve some obscurity and mystery to maintain spatial effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer swift execution for truthful detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Swift, confident execution is the best means to secure faithful and convincing detail in landscape; painstaking, mechanical little work often fails to represent natural detail properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir J. Reynolds cited that a general-character approach often produces a more faithful tree in minutes than obsessive labor on individual leaves. Swift broad handling can better suggest infinite foliage than niggling precision. But note: swift handling appropriate to landscape differs from swift handling in figure painting—do not transplant figure techniques unthinkingly to landscapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate execution principles for landscape vs figure subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles of execution appropriate to figure painting (favoring generalization) are not wholly applicable to landscape (which often requires detail and finish).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The human form often benefits from general outline and soft hues; excessive detail of hair and veins is disagreeable. Conversely, the generalizing landscape painter omits what is valuable—'thoughts, designs, and beauties by the million.' Apply different emphases depending on subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust degree of detail to picture scale and assumed foreground distance
rubrics_metrics.description: The permissible degree of generalization or detail depends on the scale of the picture and the assumed distance of the foreground from the spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote examples: miniature stippling would be offensive life-size; leaves that articulate on a 60x25ft canvas must be generalized on a 4x3ft canvas. Also consider assumed breadth of the nearest foreground (e.g., Claude often assumes a 40–50 yard breadth), which dictates how much close detail is allowable. Also account for the painter's and viewers' differing ranges of vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent the open blue sky as a deep, trembling, transparent body
rubrics_metrics.description: The open sky is not a flat color but 'a deep, quivering, transparent body'—a blue you look through rather than at; paint it in breaking, mingling, melting hues so that even a small patch remains 'spacious' and infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turner's skies are laid in breaking, mingling hues rather than flat coats. Avoid 'striking hard' against a painted dome; create penetrable depth so the eye can plunge through nearer parts into those far off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain continuity between sky and clouds (treat clouds as part of the sky)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sky should be considered as the transparent blue medium impregnated with aqueous vapor; clouds are visible spaces of that vapor, not wholly separate bodies under a dome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old masters often treated cloud and blue as distinct, causing skies to be seen 'at' rather than 'through.' Ensure cloud tones and sky tones interrelate so the sky reads as a single atmospheric mass with suspended vapors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render visible sunbeams only when physical conditions justify them
rubrics_metrics.description: Visible sunbeams arise from illuminated mist/vapor when clouds cast shadows through the vapor; beams are the sky rendered brilliant by interruption, not independent rays issuing from the sun without cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions: (1) quantity of mist dispersed through the sky is necessary; (2) broken clouds between sun and sky cause shadows that make adjacent vapor appear as beams. A ray apparent to the dazzled eye (optical artifacts) should not be painted as if physically real. Turner generally portrays beams beginning at cloud edges or in shadowed regions, not as spiky rays from the orb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modulate beam sharpness according to air/mist density
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinctness of sunbeams depends on the density of mist: denser mist gives sharp-edged rays; very clear air yields vague, gradated passages of light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rendering beams, vary edge clarity to reflect atmospheric conditions: sharp, decisive shafts for thick mist; soft, flushing passages for clearer air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid representing visionary rays seen by the dazzled eye as objective features
rubrics_metrics.description: Rays perceived by a dazzled eye (optical/subjective effects) are not real light phenomena and should generally not be represented as though physically present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworth's lines show the exception when rays appear to issue 'retired behind the mountain tops, or veiled by the dense air.' Otherwise, representing spiky rays issuing from the orb is false—older masters did this symbolically but inaccurately. Prefer showing actual light (broad blaze near the sun) and beams that begin at cloud edges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render sunset and sunrise coloring as gradual, continuous gradations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sunset colors (gold, orange, rose, purple, blue) transition gradually across the hemisphere; there are no abrupt 'belts' or discrete bands of color around the sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: Cuyp's sky with ungraduated blue, separated halo of yellow then crude pink in sharp bands is false to nature. In reality colors pass from gold into orange, orange into rose, rose into purple, purple into blue with 'absolute equality of change'—no place where 'here it changes.' Preserve smooth, continuous gradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure physical plausibility of sky colors relative to sun position and lighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Sky colors must be consistent with the sun’s position and atmospheric conditions (e.g., an impossibly dark zenith at noon or abrupt unmixed yellow at the horizon are physically impossible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Poussin's Sacrifice of Isaac shows a zenith of pitch darkness and abrupt yellow horizon at noon—'as purely impossible as color can be.' Check that upper-sky tonality, horizon tone, and sun position cohere physically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and learn from the clear, cool tones of early Italian and Dutch skies
rubrics_metrics.description: The early Italian and Dutch masters produced skies notable for clearness and coolness which are 'glorious and enviable' and serve as important ground for understanding beautiful skies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some of these qualities may be difficult to attain in modern practice, their clear tonal control is worth study; watercolors and certain older techniques achieved effects that oils often muddle—learn tonal clarity and coolness where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the relationship between clouds, shadows, and observed beam origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Beams and shafts of light typically begin where clouds end and are accounted for by cloud-cast shadows and intervening vapor; do not depict beams that contradict the positional logic of clouds and shadows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Turner: beams in the Illustrated Rogers poems begin where clouds do and are explained by cloud mass; beams should not be traced back to the sun unless an intervening cloud or mountain justifies that origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use medium-appropriate techniques: recognize differences between watercolour and oil
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain atmospheric effects (wash, sponging) achievable in watercolour produce qualities not easily reproduced in oil; one must respect the limits and affordances of the medium when aiming for particular sky or atmosphere effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While delicate, perfect skies have been produced in drawings (watercolours) by members of the Old Water Colour Society, it is not fair to compare these directly with oils. Choose techniques appropriate to your medium or adapt oil techniques to approximate wash effects carefully.
